--- title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the EU-frames case" author: "Pair: [names]" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 code-fold: false df-print: paged execute: message: false warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 --- ## The claim, and what we are doing to it The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target: > "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619) Operationalised the way that the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03. You have the data, the tools and the workflow that the project used. In Task 3 you reproduce one of the three reanalyses that worked on aggregate data, chosen by you, and from Task 4 onwards you work on the country-year panel that the facilitator built as one of the five analysts. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is how robust the published number is to *justifiable* alternative choices. Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two dots on the live class chart: an exploratory one from Task 4, and a declared one from Task 5, whose specification you fix in your preregistration before running it. ::: callout-tip ## How the tasks work Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 4 and 5, the code. The course site also has a browser version of this exercise, for practice without an installation or as a fallback if your machine fails; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Set up, and fix the vocabulary"} **First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console – it names the packages you are missing and how to install them. **Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three Rs, while one is doing something else entirely. **TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.** ***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed. ***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_? ***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_. ***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate. *(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge towards robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)* ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Meet the panel"} The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe. **TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel? euframes |> datawizard::data_summary( countries = insight::n_unique(cntry), years = insight::n_unique(year), rows = length(cntry) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. The column `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the lines first, one panel per country, then the points added on top tinyplot::tinyplot( mcosmo ~ year, facet = ~cntry, data = euframes, type = "l", col = "grey55", facet.args = list(ncol = 6), xaxb = c(2004, 2008, 2013), xlab = "", ylab = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)" ) tinyplot::tinyplot_add(type = "p", col = "black", pch = 16, cex = 0.6) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – a version of OA's Figure 1.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cosmo-trend-1.png){#fig-cosmo-trend width=864} ::: ::: Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation within each country over time is what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses. *Downloading from OSF (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way that a researcher would, with a course-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it gives you practice in downloading a published file from its repository: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline). source("R/get_data.R") ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph"} Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model. **TODO – complete the estimand statement:** > Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\]. *(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country from one year to another, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)* Next come the identification assumptions: the claims about what causes what that must hold for the coefficient to be read as the effect of unemployment. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `dagify()`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula written the way you read a regression, effect on the left of the tilde and cause on the right. `framing ~ unemployment` is therefore the arrow unemployment → framing. The causal path and the two confounder pairs are switched on; the arguable arrows are in the same call, commented out with a `#`, each with a line of justification above it. Open the file, take the `#` off any arrow you believe, re-source, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`. A node appears in the plot only once some arrow mentions it, so the plot shows only the arrows that are switched on and the nodes that they join. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/dag_starter.R") plot_dag(dag) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders.](index_files/figure-html/dag-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect? dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { country, year } ``` ::: ::: For the starter graph the adjustment set is `{ country, year }`, which is what the two-way fixed effects that you fit in Task 3 absorb. Country fixed effects adjust for `country` and year fixed effects for `year`, so the DAG and the model encode the same identification claim. **TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:** 1. What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)* 2. What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)* Whatever set is returned by your DAG becomes field 4 of the preregistration you write in Task 5. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce a recorded result"} This is the **reproducibility** check. Three of the five Multi100 analysts fitted their models on aggregate data, and their recorded results reproduce exactly from files in `data/`. The other two, KEVF1 and PRL47, fitted theirs on several hundred thousand respondents, whose files GESIS does not allow this workspace to hold. **Choose one of the three**, work through its chunk line by line, and compare the *t* that you get with the value on record. The chunks of the other two run as well when the report renders, so that you can set the three side by side afterwards. The codebooks in `data/` say how each file was built. | Analyst | Data | Model | On record | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | C6HJR | `EUframes_cy.csv`, 270 country-years | Two-way fixed effects (country and year), conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df | | KQXUE | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years | Country fixed effects, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df | | 018OL | `analyst_018OL.csv`, 420 cells of country, year and wave | Random intercepts for country, year and wave, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom | t = −1.206 on 396.9 df | **TODO:** the analyst you chose, the *t* and degrees of freedom you obtained, and one sentence on how the model of that analyst differs from the other two: ........... **C6HJR.** Cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with fixed effects for country and year, on the course panel. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Grand-mean centre unemployment, as the submitted analysis did. With # two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it # is the transformation that the recorded specification uses, so do it # explicitly. euframes <- euframes |> datawizard::data_modify(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE)) # fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects. m1 <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes, vcov = "iid") parameters::model_parameters(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: **KQXUE.** The cosmopolitan share of each respondent's mentions, averaged by country and year as the Stata code of the analyst averages it, on unemployment as a share of the population aged 20–64, with a fixed effect for each country and none for the year. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kqxue <- readr::read_csv("data/analyst_KQXUE.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) # xtreg cosmo unemployment, fe in Stata: country effects only, conventional errors m_kqxue <- fixest::feols(cosmo ~ unemp | cntry, data = kqxue, vcov = "iid") parameters::model_parameters(m_kqxue) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: **018OL.** The mean of the five cosmopolitan items, averaged in cells of country, year and wave, on the unemployment rate of those aged 15–74, with random intercepts for country, year and wave. The analyst rescaled the outcome to run from 0 to 1 before fitting, which changes the coefficient but neither *t* nor the degrees of freedom. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} o18ol <- readr::read_csv("data/analyst_018OL.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> datawizard::data_modify(pos01 = datawizard::rescale(pos, to = c(0, 1))) # lme4 fits the model; lmerTest adds the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom m_018ol <- lmerTest::lmer(pos01 ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | year) + (1 | wave), data = o18ol) parameters::model_parameters(m_018ol, effects = "fixed", ci_method = "satterthwaite") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-corrected .cell tbl-cap='The three reproductions on aggregate data.'} ```{.r .cell-code} modelsummary::modelsummary( list("C6HJR" = m1, "KQXUE" = m_kqxue, "018OL" = m_018ol), estimate = "{estimate}", statistic = "t = {statistic}", gof_map = "nobs", coef_map = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment", "unemp" = "Unemployment") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
C6HJR KQXUE 018OL
Unemployment -0.003 -0.007 -0.002
t = -3.804 t = -7.169 t = -1.206
Num.Obs. 270 270 420
``` ::: ::: Each model returns the value on record to the third decimal: **t = −3.804** for C6HJR, **t = −7.169** for KQXUE and **t = −1.206** for 018OL. The argument `vcov = "iid"` asks for classical standard errors, which assume that the errors are independent and identically distributed; they are the kind that `plm` reported for C6HJR and `xtreg` for KQXUE, which is why the *t* values match to three decimals. The three numbers are far apart although all three analysts worked on the same claim. They differ in what they averaged, which series of unemployment they took, which effects they removed and which errors they computed, and the case study on the course site sets the differences out. The data files carry two slips that the case study describes, both kept so that the values on record come back: the Stata code of KQXUE appended EB 62.0 twice (`cosmo_once` is the mean without the duplicate), and the files of 018OL put EB 79.3, fielded in 2013, in 2012 (`year_fieldwork` has the true year). Part 4 shows what changes when the country-years are not treated as independent. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproduction and the five analysts"} You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the class who chose the same analyst, because each of you ran the same code on the same file. That is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish once the data and the code are in hand; for these three analyses, putting them in hand meant rebuilding two of the files from the code that the analysts deposited. The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different numbers, one of them not significant under the analyst's own test. Part of the spread comes from the questions that each analyst chose to answer, part from errors that only a reading of the code shows, and most of the spread in the recorded correlations from the conversion that put them on one scale, as the case study on the course site sets out. In Task 2 you named the quantity you are after and drew the graph from which your adjustment set follows. In Task 4 you will see how far the answer moves when the other choices change. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Work the menu"} This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. The specification that you submit with `submit_exploration()` at the end of this task is labelled exploratory on the class chart. The one labelled declared is fixed later, in the preregistration cell of Task 5, before it is run. Both carry the tag that `submit_exploration()` prints, such as `amber-otter-42`, which is kept in the file `.class-tag` of this workspace and lets you find your own marks on the chart. To choose your own, write `submit_exploration(nickname = "...")` with a nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the specification menu. Every argument defaults to the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR in Task 3, on which the menu and the curve are built, so changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays as it is in that model. Every call is a real fit on your machine. The arguments for the decisions about the question change the question, the measurement arguments select which version of the country-year panel is fitted (which items the outcome was built from, whether its cells were weighted, what was done with respondents who mentioned nothing, which published series supplies the predictor), and the arguments for the decisions about the model set the form of the predictor. The printout gives the slope `b` with its conventional standard error and *t*, the claim-aligned partial *r*, the p-value of the test that classes every point on the curve, the class of the result and its placement among the 864 specifications on the curve of the claim. That test allows the years of one country to be correlated with one another, which the conventional *t* does not. It clusters the standard errors by country with the CR2 correction, which suits a small number of countries of unequal weight, and judges the *t* against Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which count how many countries effectively carry the information; both are computed on your machine with each fit, by the `clubSandwich` package. The reproduced specification lies below zero, but with a CR2 p of 0.0504 on 9.8 Satterthwaite degrees of freedom it is not significant at 5%, and 67% of the 864 specifications lie further in the direction of the claim. The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Every other option is still an argument of `try_spec()`, and trying one is part of the exercise: the helper refuses it, gives the reason why it is not on the curve, and names the page of the course site that teaches it. **TODO:** run the six calls below and the refused one after them, then write your own. Three or four of your own is plenty. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec() # the reproduced specification itself ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00347 se = 0.00091 t = -3.804 on 233 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.242, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0504 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 9.8 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero, but not significant under CR2 (p >= 0.05) Placement: 67% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(outcome = "mpos") # the composite of both positive framings ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpos ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00485 se = 0.00097 t = -4.986 on 233 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.311, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0103 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 9.8 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero and significant under CR2 (p < 0.05), in the direction of the claim Placement: 51% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(estimator = "fe_country") # country effects only: changes common to all of Europe stay in ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_country | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00564 se = 0.00082 t = -6.869 on 242 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.404, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0072 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 8.5 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero and significant under CR2 (p < 0.05), in the direction of the claim Placement: 28% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(predictor = "growth") # GDP growth instead of unemployment, in the World Bank series ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ growth(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_growth | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00108 se = 0.00095 t = -1.137 on 233 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.074, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.5607 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 10.0 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero, but not significant under CR2 (p >= 0.05) Placement: 96% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (growth: b, t and r are shown with their signs flipped, because the claim expects framing to rise with growth) (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(copredictor = "other") # adjusted for the other economic measure, here GDP growth ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) + growth | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00356 se = 0.00098 t = -3.621 on 232 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.231, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0269 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 10.0 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero and significant under CR2 (p < 0.05), in the direction of the claim Placement: 70% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(noop = "drop") # leave out the respondents who mentioned no frame ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, drop, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00466 se = 0.00093 t = -5.009 on 233 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.312, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0134 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 9.8 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero and significant under CR2 (p < 0.05), in the direction of the claim Placement: 50% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(measure = "es_2064_pop") # a Eurostat unemployment series instead of the World Bank one ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, es_2064_pop | gaussian, se:cr2] b = -0.00431 se = 0.00121 t = -3.555 on 233 df (conventional standard error) partial r = -0.227, claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim) p = 0.0692 with CR2 errors clustered by country, on 9.6 Satterthwaite df Class: below zero, but not significant under CR2 (p >= 0.05) Placement: 72% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r (fitted live, with CR2 and its Satterthwaite df computed here by clubSandwich) ``` ::: ::: The first four calls change the question that is being asked of the data; the last two keep the question and change only how it is measured. The next chunk asks for an option that is not on the curve. It stops with the reason, and the report still renders because the chunk is marked `error: true`. Edit it to try others, such as `sample = "no_bailout"`, `weights = "pop"`, `construction = "count"`, `family = "beta"` or `outcome = "mneg"`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl") # pooled OLS: refused, with the reason why ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! estimator = "pooled_cl" (Pooled OLS) is not on the curve of 864 specifications, so it has no result here. Why: Mixes the stable differences between countries with change within them; on these data the two run in opposite directions, so the pooled slope answers neither reading of the claim. Where it is taught: The statistical methods behind the course, https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/companion/stats-methods.html Every decision and its options: Decision map, https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/cases/eu-frames/map.html To stay on the curve, choose estimator = "fe_twoway" or "fe_country". ``` ::: ::: Everything you try is logged. Print the log to see the small multiverse you have just built. Only the decisions that you varied are shown, which keeps the comparison readable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_experiments() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Specifications you have tried (7): outcome predictor copredictor estimator noop measure b t mcosmo unemp none fe_twoway zero wb_nat -0.00347 -3.80 mpos unemp none fe_twoway zero wb_nat -0.00485 -4.99 mcosmo unemp none fe_country zero wb_nat -0.00564 -6.87 mcosmo growth none fe_twoway zero wb_growth -0.00108 -1.14 mcosmo unemp other fe_twoway zero wb_nat -0.00356 -3.62 mcosmo unemp none fe_twoway drop wb_nat -0.00466 -5.01 mcosmo unemp none fe_twoway zero es_2064_pop -0.00431 -3.56 r_aligned p_cr2 -0.242 0.0504 -0.311 0.0103 -0.404 0.0072 -0.074 0.5607 -0.231 0.0269 -0.312 0.0134 -0.227 0.0692 Spread of claim-aligned r: -0.404 to -0.074 | below zero and significant under CR2: 4 of 7 ``` ::: ::: When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} submit_exploration() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why label it 'exploratory'?"} You chose this specification after seeing what several of them do, so it lacks the guarantee carried by a choice that is fixed in a preregistration before it is run: it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out. Almost no published paper reports which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. The class chart does, because everyone submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after preregistering a specification, so the two sets of dots can be read against each other. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"} A preregistration fixes your specification **before** you know its result, which stops you from quietly picking the one that happens to give the answer you wanted. In a real study it is filed, with a date stamp, in a public registry such as the OSF. In this report the preregistration is the cell below, and the code enforces it: the R session keeps the choices that you set in that cell, every later cell reads them, and `build_model()` refuses model code that departs from them. Make one choice on each decision of the specification menu, then run the cell. The menu has fourteen decisions in three groups. The seven decisions about the question fix what you are asking, the four measurement decisions fix how that question is measured, and the three decisions about the model fix how it is estimated. The curve of 864 specifications keeps two or more options on nine of these decisions and a single option on the other five, which are the sample, the weighting, the scoring rule, the model family and the inference. An option that is not on the curve stops `prereg()` with the reason why, as it stops `try_spec()`. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the course convention, applied automatically: the claim expects framing to rise with GDP growth, so the sign of a growth slope is flipped, and 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone. Task 2 of Multi100 fixed unemployment as the measure; the curve also holds GDP growth. In Task 1 of Multi100, where the choice was left to them, four of the five analysts already used GDP growth, two of them beside unemployment. ::: ::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"} *A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ============================================================================ # MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result # ============================================================================ # 1.
